title: Conduct Logging and Monitoring Activities
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 7: Security Operations: Conduct Logging and Monitoring Activities.

items: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) — monitors and alerts on suspicious activity; passive — does not take direct action
IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) — monitors and blocks suspicious activity; active — placed inline with traffic
NIDS/NIPS — network-based; monitors network traffic at strategic points (e.g., network perimeter, DMZ boundaries)
HIDS/HIPS — host-based; monitors activity on individual systems (file changes, registry modifications, system calls)

rows: Compares traffic/activity against known attack patterns
Establishes baseline of normal activity, alerts on deviations
Uses rules and algorithms to identify suspicious behavior

items: False positive — alert triggered but no actual attack occurred
False negative — actual attack occurred but IDS/IPS failed to detect it (more dangerous)
Place IDS/IPS sensors at: network perimeter, between network segments, on critical servers

blocks.text: An IDS, as the name suggests, is a detection system. It examines traffic at the network level or host level, specifically looking for malicious activity, policy violations, or other signs of suspicious activity and can alert and/or log those events. An IDS does not take direct action against the traffic. An IPS, by contrast, is placed inline with traffic and can actively block or prevent detected threats. The trade-off is that a misconfigured IPS can block legitimate traffic (causing a denial of service to valid users). The key distinction between signature-based and anomaly-based detection is critical for the exam. A signature-based IDS can only detect known threats — if the attack signature is not in its database, the attack will go undetected. An anomaly-based IDS (also known as behavior-based) can detect new security threats because it looks for deviations from established baselines, but it generates more false positives because legitimate but unusual activity may trigger alerts. NIST SP 800-94 provides detailed guidance on intrusion detection and prevention systems. ⚠️ Exam Trap: If the question asks what can detect "new" or "unknown" attacks, the answer is anomaly-based (behavior-based) IDS, NOT signature-based. Signature-based only detects KNOWN attack patterns.

items: SIEM combines SIM (Security Information Management) and SEM (Security Event Management)
Aggregation — collects log data from multiple sources (firewalls, IDS/IPS, servers, applications, endpoints)
Correlation — discovers relationships between events across different sources to identify complex attack patterns
Normalization — converts logs from different formats into a consistent format for analysis
Alerting — generates alerts based on correlation rules, thresholds, and anomaly detection
Dashboards and reporting — provides real-time visibility and compliance reporting
Retention — stores logs for forensic analysis and compliance requirements
Reduces the volume of data analysts must review by correlating events and highlighting significant patterns

blocks.text: The volume of log data generated by modern IT environments makes manual review impractical. A SIEM system addresses this by aggregating logs from disparate sources, normalizing them into a common format, and applying correlation rules to identify patterns that may indicate security incidents. Correlation is perhaps the most valuable SIEM capability. For example, a login from a unique geographic location at an unusual time might be individually unremarkable, but when correlated with a concurrent password change and data download, it could indicate account compromise. This deviation from the norm is a correlation that can easily be detected as an anomaly. SIEM systems also support compliance by providing automated reporting capabilities for frameworks like PCI DSS, HIPAA, and SOX, which require demonstrable log monitoring and retention.

items: Ongoing assessment of security controls and organizational risk posture
Includes real-time monitoring of security events, configuration changes, and vulnerability status
NIST SP 800-137 provides guidance on Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM)
Key components: vulnerability scanning, configuration monitoring, network monitoring, log analysis
Feeds into the risk management process by providing current security status information
Egress monitoring — monitoring outbound traffic to detect data exfiltration or unauthorized communications
DLP (Data Loss Prevention) — tools that detect and prevent unauthorized transfer of sensitive data
DLP operates at three points: endpoint (USB, print, clipboard), network (email, web, FTP), and storage (file shares, databases)
Computer lockdowns prevent writing sensitive data to non-company-owned storage devices (e.g., USB drives)
Monitor for: unauthorized email of sensitive data, upload to cloud storage, printing of classified documents
Audit trails — records created by logging events and occurrences; used to reconstruct events, extract information about incidents, and prove or disprove culpability
Clipping levels — thresholds that define the baseline of acceptable activity; events exceeding the threshold trigger alerts
Log protection — logs must be protected from unauthorized modification; only administrators should have delete access
Logs should capture: who (user/system), what (action), when (timestamp), where (source/destination), outcome (success/failure)
Log retention — define retention periods based on regulatory requirements and organizational policy
NTP synchronization — all systems must have synchronized time for accurate log correlation
NIST SP 800-92 provides guidance on managing log data securely

blocks.text: Audit trails provide a passive form of detective security control. They are the records created by recording information about events and occurrences into one or more databases or log files, and they can be used to reconstruct events, extract information about incidents, and prove or disprove culpability. Clipping levels are widely used in auditing to establish a baseline of routine system or user activity. The monitoring system raises an alarm to signal abnormal events only after the clipping level threshold is exceeded. For example, rather than alerting on every single failed login attempt, the system counts the failures and locks the account only when a predefined threshold is reached (e.g., 5 failed attempts). Two forms of log sampling exist:

items: Statistical sampling — uses mathematically random methods to select a representative sample from the audit log population
Nonstatistical (clipping) — focuses on specific events exceeding defined thresholds; less expensive and easier to implement but may miss events below the threshold

blocks.text: NIST SP 800-92 outlines a set of critical requirements for securely managing log data, including defining auditable events, establishing log management processes, and implementing log protection mechanisms. ⚠️ Exam Trap: Clipping is a form of nonstatistical sampling that reduces logged data based on a threshold. Statistical sampling uses random methods. Don't confuse the two.

items: Threat intelligence — evidence-based knowledge about existing or emerging threats
Requires understanding of both vulnerabilities (that can be exploited) and threats (actors/events that exploit them)
Sources: open-source intelligence (OSINT), commercial feeds, government sharing (ISACs), dark web monitoring
MITRE ATT&CK Framework — comprehensive knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques; organizes techniques by tactic categories (e.g., Reconnaissance, Initial Access, Execution)
Threat hunting — proactive search for threats that have evaded existing security controls
Intelligence feeds are integrated into SIEM and SOAR platforms for automated correlation

blocks.text: Risk-based security requires a holistic understanding of risk, comprising vulnerabilities that can be exploited by threats. Security practices like patch management focus on identifying and addressing vulnerabilities, but threat intelligence adds the other dimension — understanding who might attack, what techniques they use, and what they're after. The MITRE ATT&CK Framework is an increasingly important resource. It catalogs the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used by attackers. The framework organizes techniques by tactic (the "why" — e.g., Reconnaissance, Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation) and each tactic contains multiple techniques (the "how"). Some techniques include subtechniques for more granular detail. This framework is useful for both offensive (red team) and defensive (blue team) operations.

items: SOAR — Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response
Orchestration — integrates multiple security tools and processes into a unified workflow
Automation — automates repetitive tasks (e.g., alert triage, enrichment, containment actions)
Response — implements predefined playbooks for incident response
SOAR platforms can automatically detect and respond to incidents, reducing mean time to respond (MTTR)
Reduces analyst fatigue by automating low-level, repetitive tasks
Integrates with SIEM, threat intelligence, ticketing systems, firewalls, EDR
